tests.title: Severity
tests.text: Does the gap narrow for crimes that reach police anyway? It widens: against White women from 9.7x for simple assault without serious injury to 23.3x for assaults with a gun, and against Hispanic women from 3.1x to 8x. Homicide: 80 Black women and 5 White women were killed, 12.7x (95% CI 5.2 to 40.3), too few to chart. Asian women are left out of the chart: only 5 were victims of assault with a gun. Bars need 10 victims in the comparison group.
tests.ytitle: Black women's rate as a multiple

reporting.title: Reporting: partly testable
reporting.text: If the gap came from Black women reporting more, it would narrow for the crimes reported most often, and it widens instead (Severity, above). Nationally, 40% of simple assaults reach police against 75% of crimes involving a gun, and reporting differs little by race: 51% of violent crimes against Black victims and 48% against White victims in 2024 (56% and 42% in 2023). For reporting alone to make the 10.2x gap, White women would have to report under 10% of assaults even if Black women reported all of them. Unreported assaults stay invisible here.

sections.title: Neighborhood and income
sections.note: NIBRS has no location. MPD's public incident data has locations but no victim race. This section places 4,741 assaults with a dangerous weapon from 2022 to 2025 in census tracts and averages each tract's rate per resident over where each group's women live. It describes places, not victims.

boxes.title: Where women live, by tract poverty
boxes.text: 43.1% of Black women live in tracts where 25% or more of residents are poor, against 6.2% of White women. Citywide, 26.3% of Black women are below the poverty line, against 5.1% of White women, and median household income is $60,764 for Black households and $170,201 for White ones.

boxes.title: Recorded violence by tract poverty
boxes.text: Tracts where 25% or more of residents are poor record 3.55 assaults with a dangerous weapon per 1,000 residents a year, against 0.79 in tracts under 10%. Averaged over where women live, Black women's tracts record 2.8x the rate of White women's and 2x Hispanic women's.

datasets.label: Assaults with a dangerous weapon per 1,000 residents a year

findings.title: What this check says
findings.text: If every woman faced her own tract's rate, Black women's aggravated assault rate would be 2.8x White women's and 2x Hispanic women's. It is 14.4x and 4.7x. Neighborhood accounts for a factor of about 2.8 against White women; a factor of about 5.2 remains that this check cannot place. Other definitions give a smaller neighborhood factor: 1.8x counting all violent crime, 2x per square kilometer.

findings.title: What it cannot say
findings.text: These are tract averages, not victims. Neighbors on different blocks can face different risks, and assaults away from home are not placed. Neighborhood poverty is shaped by segregation and discrimination, so the part of the gap found in neighborhoods is located, not explained away.

findings.title: National context
findings.text: The national crime survey, which counts crimes whether or not they were reported, finds similar rates of violence for Black and White people: 23.4 and 22.1 per 1,000 in 2024, both sexes. Poor urban Black and White residents had similar rates too (51.3 and 56.4 per 1,000, 2008 to 2012).

sections.title: Protection: are cases cleared by arrest equally?
sections.note: Written down before it was run (docs/clearance-test-plan.md). An arrest within 90 days of the incident, from MPD's arrest records in the same NIBRS files, for women victims, compared inside each relationship and assault type, because DC law requires an arrest in domestic and family cases when there is probable cause.

boxes.title: Arrest within 90 days, by relationship
boxes.text: In partner assaults, 44.1% of Black women's cases end in an arrest within 90 days, against 59.2% of White women's and 57.3% of Hispanic women's. Among strangers: 41.1%, 38.4% and 36.7%. Asian women are left out of the chart: 289 victims in all.

boxes.title: Compared like with like
boxes.text: Black women's arrest rate as a multiple of each group's, inside each relationship (below 1 means less often). All relationships together, compared like with like: 0.9x (95% CI 0.85 to 0.96) against White women, 0.86x (95% CI 0.81 to 0.9) against Hispanic women.

findings.title: What the test says
findings.text: Both comparisons are mixed by the rule written before the test. Compared like with like, Black women's cases end in an arrest 0.9 times as often as White women's (95% CI 0.85 to 0.96) and 0.86 times as often as Hispanic women's (95% CI 0.81 to 0.9). The gap sits in partner and other family assaults: in partner assaults, 0.74 times as often as White women's (95% CI 0.69 to 0.81). There is no clear difference for stranger or unknown relationships. It holds in both halves of the window. Against White women it sits in same-day arrests (0.88x), not later ones (1.06x).

findings.title: Why the raw rates mislead
findings.text: Before comparing like with like, Black women's cases look more likely to end in an arrest (38.4% against 33.4% for White women). More of them are partner assaults (32.7% against 22.0%), where DC Code 16-1031 requires an arrest when there is probable cause, and fewer have an unknown relationship (18.5% against 41.9%), where arrests are rare.

findings.title: How cases close without an arrest
findings.text: Cases with Black women victims are closed as "victim refused to cooperate" 2.1 times as often as White women's (95% CI 1.54 to 2.87), like with like (6.4% against 1.9% before adjusting). That is the reason police recorded. It cannot separate a victim's choice, or her safety, from how the case was handled.

findings.title: What it cannot say
findings.text: Clearance is not a measure of police effort. It depends on whether the person who did it was still there, whether there was probable cause, the victim's cooperation and the evidence. Nothing here measures offenders.
